Bass / Reading tablature

Read a tab and know what to play.

Lines tell you the strings, numbers tell you the frets, and rhythm tells you when. Read two short examples, then decode the common technique symbols.

Try it on the fretboard ↗

Understand

Follow time from left to right. A 0 means an open string; 2 means the second fret, not your second finger. Numbers directly above each other belong to the same moment. A blank string line does not tell you to play that string.

Standard four-string tuning: E A D G, from the thickest string to the thinnest.

From the neck to the tab

Follow string 1 through the three views. The instrument stays the same; only the drawing turns.

Cyan: string 1. Pink: the last string. The numbers are frets, not fingers. Only the numbered string is played.

Make the connection

A simple text tab often leaves note lengths unclear. Tab with stems, beams, rests or a rhythmic staff can specify them precisely. Do not infer rhythm just from the spacing of typed numbers. Check the time signature, tempo, tuning and capo instruction before starting a new score.

Play it

In bar 1, play the open first string, fret 2, then fret 3, one beat each. Stop the sound for beat 4. In bar 2, the first two notes take half a beat each; the next takes one beat and the final open string lasts two beats.

Treat the top count as a ruler. Every bar here totals four beats. A half-beat note occupies half the distance of a one-beat note. First clap the rhythm, then speak the string and fret, then play. The text version below provides the same instructions without relying on the drawing.

Four lines, from top to bottom: G D A E. Pluck one note at a time and stop unused strings with either hand. The end of a note is as important as its attack.

A worked example

Read left to right. Counts above mark the beats; numbers on the lines are frets; numbers below give the duration in beats. R = rest. Stacked fret numbers sound together. Start at 60 BPM.

Read the example as text
  1. Bar 1
    1. String 1 (G), Fret 0, G · 1 beats
    2. String 1 (G), Fret 2, A · 1 beats
    3. String 1 (G), Fret 3, A♯ · 1 beats
    4. Rest · 1 beats
  2. Bar 2
    1. String 1 (G), Fret 0, G · ½ beats
    2. String 1 (G), Fret 2, A · ½ beats
    3. String 1 (G), Fret 3, A♯ · 1 beats
    4. String 1 (G), Fret 0, G · 2 beats

Common tablature symbols

SymbolHow to play it
0Play the open string.
xTouch the string without fretting a pitch and strike a muted note; this is not a rest.
5h7Pick fret 5, then hammer onto fret 7 on the same string without picking again.
7p5Hold fret 5 ready; play 7, then release it with a controlled pull to sound 5.
5/7 · 7\5Keep contact with the string and slide to the written destination fret.
7b9 · rBend the note at fret 7 until it reaches the pitch of fret 9; r means release the bend.
~Vibrato: vary the pitch around the held note.
P.M.Lightly damp the strings near the bridge with the picking-hand palm.
RIn these exercises, stop the sound for the stated duration.
| · :||A bar line divides measures; a repeat sign sends you back to the matching repeat start or the beginning.

A mistake to avoid

A hyphen in plain text tab is usually a string line, not an instruction to stop. A missing number is not an open string. If a capo is specified, check whether fret numbers are relative to it; do not silently mix capo and nut positions.

Listen and check

Count 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & before playing. In the second bar, the last note starts on beat 3 and continues through beat 4. Do not pluck it again on 4.

Ready for the next step?

Read both bars without reversing the strings, explain why 0 is played but R is silent, and sustain the final note for two beats. Then identify a hammer-on, a pull-off and a slide in the table.
